title: At the Cafe: Pastries and Light Food
summary: Cafes sell more than drinks. Many also sell pastries and light food such as croissants, muffins, sandwiches, salads, and toasties.

cover.alt: A cafe table shows a butter croissant, blueberry muffin, cheese toastie, and garden salad in soft daylight.

blocks.title: Pastries and Light Food at a Cafe
paragraphs: Cafes sell more than drinks. Many also sell pastries and light food such as croissants, muffins, sandwiches, salads, and toasties. Knowing a few food words helps you order clearly and feel ready. You will read about cafe food options and how to order them, then practise in three short conversations.

items.prompt: Do you like sweet food or savoury food at a cafe?
items.answer: Open answer. For example: I like sweet food, especially muffins.
items.explanation: Cafes often sell both sweet pastries and savoury sandwiches.

items.prompt: What light food do you usually buy with a drink?
items.answer: Open answer. For example: I usually buy a croissant or a sandwich.
items.explanation: Many people order food and a drink together.

items.prompt: Can you name one pastry you know?
items.answer: Open answer. For example: A croissant, a muffin, or a danish.
items.explanation: Pastries are baked goods that people often eat in the morning.

blocks.title: Cafe Pastries and Light Food
paragraphs: Many cafes keep a glass case of pastries near the counter. A butter croissant is flaky and light. A blueberry muffin is soft and sweet. Some places also sell a cheese danish or a cinnamon roll. These cafe pastries are popular in the morning with tea or coffee.

Light food is good when you want more than a snack but not a big meal. A chicken sandwich is easy to eat with your hands. A cheese toastie is a hot sandwich with melted cheese. A garden salad is cooler and lighter. At places like Pret A Manger, people often grab a sandwich or a salad to eat for lunch. You can ask what is fresh today, or point to the item you want in the case.

items.prompt: Name two pastries and two light food items you might find at a cafe.
items.answer: Pastries can include a butter croissant and a blueberry muffin. Light food can include a chicken sandwich, a cheese toastie, or a garden salad.
items.explanation:
Pastries are usually sweet or flaky baked goods. Light food is a small meal such as a sandwich or salad.

Which of these would you choose for lunch?

rows.term: What pastries do you have today?
rows.meaning: You ask which baked items are available now.
rows.example: What pastries do you have today? I want a sweet pastry.

rows.meaning: You ask if the muffin was baked recently.
rows.example: Is the muffin fresh? I prefer soft ones.

rows.term: I would like a cheese toastie, please.
rows.meaning: A polite way to order a hot cheese sandwich.
rows.example: I would like a cheese toastie, please. For here.

rows.term: Can I see the salad options?
rows.meaning: You ask the barista to show or list the salads.
rows.example: Can I see the salad options? I want a light meal.

blocks.title: How to Order Food at a Cafe
paragraphs: Ordering food at a cafe follows a simple pattern. The barista greets you. You say the food item clearly. Then the barista may ask if you want it heated, or ask for here or to go.

Keep the order short. Say the full dish name as one unit, such as butter croissant or garden salad. If you want a change, add it after the item: no butter, extra cheese, or no onion. After that, the barista tells you the price. You pay, then wait for your name or for the food at the counter.
You can order food alone, or add a simple drink if you want. Practise the food words clearly before you add extras.

items.prompt: What should you say first when you order food at a cafe?
items.answer: Say the food item clearly, using the full dish name. Then add any change, such as heated or no onion.
items.explanation:
A clear dish name helps the barista find the right item quickly.

What is one change you might ask for with a sandwich?

rows.term: Can you heat that up, please?
rows.meaning: You ask the barista to warm the food.
rows.example: A cheese toastie, please. Can you heat that up, please?

rows.meaning: The barista asks if you will eat inside or take the food away.
rows.example: For here or to go? To go, please.

rows.meaning: You ask the barista to leave onion out of the food.
rows.example: A chicken sandwich, please. No onion, please.
How much is that? I will pay by card.

blocks.title: Changes, Extras, and Paying
paragraphs: After you name the food, you can ask for a small change. Say no onion, extra cheese, or no butter. If the food is cold, you can ask the barista to heat it up. These short lines keep the order clear.

When the food is ready, the barista may call your name or bring it to the counter. You can pay by card or with cash. If you also want a drink, say the food first, then the drink. Keep each part short so the barista can repeat the order back to you.

items.prompt: When should you say a change like no onion or heat that up?
items.answer: Say the change after you name the food item, so the barista knows exactly what to make.
items.explanation:
The dish name comes first. Then add one short change.

What payment method do you usually use at a cafe?

rows.meaning: You ask for more cheese on the food.
rows.example: A cheese toastie with extra cheese, please.

rows.meaning: You ask the barista to leave sauce out of the food.
rows.example: A chicken sandwich, please. No sauce, please.

rows.meaning: You tell the barista you will use a bank card.
rows.example: How much is that? I will pay by card.

rows.meaning: You ask the barista to say the order or price again.
rows.example: Could you repeat that? I did not catch the price.

blocks.title: Scene: Ordering a Pastry
paragraphs: You are at a bright cafe counter in the morning. A glass case shows butter croissants and blueberry muffins. The barista, Maya, is waiting with a smile.
You want a pastry for breakfast. You are not sure which one is freshest, so you plan to ask.
Your goal is to ask about the pastries, choose one, and finish the order.

images.alt: A smiling barista stands behind a glass case of croissants and muffins while greeting a morning customer.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Good morning! What can I get for you today?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Good morning. What pastries do you have today?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: We have butter croissants and blueberry muffins. Both are fresh this morning.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Is the muffin soft?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes. The blueberry muffin is soft and sweet.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I would like a blueberry muffin, please.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Sure. For here or to go?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: For here, please. How much is that?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That is three fifty. I will bring it over in a moment.

blocks.title: Scene: Ordering a Toastie
paragraphs: It is time for lunch. You return to the same cafe. The board lists a cheese toastie and a chicken sandwich. The barista, Leo, is behind the counter.
You want a warm savoury snack. You also want to ask if the toastie can be heated.
Your goal is to order a cheese toastie, ask for it heated, and say if it is for here or to go.

images.alt: A barista presents a hot cheese toastie on a plate at a sunlit midday cafe counter.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Hi there. Ready to order?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes. I would like a cheese toastie, please.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Good choice. Would you like it heated?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, please. Can you heat that up?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: Of course. For here or to go?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: To go, please.

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: No problem. Anything else?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, that is all. How much is that?

turns.speaker: Leo
turns.text: That is five twenty. It will be ready in a few minutes.

blocks.title: Scene: Ordering a Salad and Sandwich
paragraphs: Later in the afternoon, you want a lighter meal. The cafe sells a garden salad and a chicken sandwich. The barista, Sam, is free at the counter.
You want the chicken sandwich with no onion, and you may add a small drink if it feels natural.
Your goal is to order the chicken sandwich with no onion, confirm for here or to go, and complete payment.

images.alt: A barista presents a chicken sandwich and a fresh garden salad at an afternoon cafe counter.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Welcome back. What would you like?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Can I see the salad options?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Today we have a garden salad, or a chicken sandwich if you want a more filling option.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I will have the chicken sandwich, please. No onion, please.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Got it. No onion. For here or to go?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: For here, please. And a small tea with that.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Sure. One chicken sandwich with no onion, and a small tea.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How much is that?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: That is seven eighty. I will call you when it is ready.

items.prompt: Imagine you are at a cafe. What pastry or light food do you want? Practise your order out loud. Use at least two phrases from the lesson.
items.answer: Open answer. For example: I would like a cheese toastie, please. Can you heat that up, please? To go.
items.explanation: Try to include the full dish name and one clear request such as heated or no onion.

items.prompt: Cafes sell pastries like croissants and muffins, and light food like sandwiches, toasties, and salads. Saying the full dish name and any change makes ordering easy. Which cafe food would you order next, and why?
items.answer: Open answer. For example: I would order a butter croissant because it is light and good in the morning.
items.explanation: There is no wrong answer. Use the food words from the lesson.

items.prompt: What phrase would you use to ask the barista to warm your food?
items.answer: Can you heat that up, please?
items.explanation: This short phrase is polite and clear.

rows.example: I ordered a butter croissant with my tea.

rows.meaning: A soft, sweet cake baked in a small round shape.
rows.example: The blueberry muffin was still warm.

rows.meaning: A hot toasted sandwich, often with melted cheese.
rows.example: A cheese toastie is perfect on a cold day.

rows.meaning: A person who works at a cafe and takes your order.
rows.example: The barista asked if I wanted the sandwich heated.

rows.meaning: Food or drink that you take away instead of eating in the cafe.
rows.example: For here or to go? To go, please.
